F4RM — Robustness Ablations (E6–E11)¶

Notebook 2 of 3: Six robustness sweeps probing whether the F4RM advantage survives perturbations to bleach threshold, thermometer choice, storage backend, ensemble size and composition, RAM selection, and per-dataset hyperparameter tuning.

Companion notebooks:

  • F4RM_01_Foundations_and_Headline.ipynb — concept + E1–E5 headline
  • F4RM_03_Comparisons_and_Pareto.ipynb — Section 4 Pareto vs baselines + prior weightless systems

How this notebook is organized¶

  • 3.1 — E6: Bleach threshold sweep (does the win survive non-default bleach?)
  • 3.2 — E7: Thermometer encoding sweep (Linear / Distributive / Gaussian / Exponential / Stochastic)
  • 3.3 — E8: Storage backend memory comparison (Dense hashmap vs Cuckoo filter)
  • 3.4 — E9a: F4RMS K-sweep (does the gap widen as K grows?)
  • 3.4 — E9b: Heterogeneous-a F4RMS (mixed a values vs homogeneous)
  • 3.5 — E10: RAM selection (validation-driven and Fisher-score selection)
  • 3.6 — E11: Per-dataset hyperparameter tuning grid (full sweep)

All cells load from notebooks/cache/E*_results.pkl and paper_tables/E*.csv.

3.1 — E6: Bleach threshold sweep¶

Bleach (β) is the threshold below which a RAM count is treated as zero during inference. β=1 (the default) treats any RAM that ever fired as informative; larger β requires more train-time co-occurrences before counting toward inference.

This sweep tests whether F4RM's advantage over Random survives across β ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16}. Result: F4RM > Random at every β.

3.2 — E7: Thermometer encoding sweep¶

Five thermometer variants, all tested with both Random and F4RM mappings:

  • Linear: equally-spaced thresholds between min and max
  • Distributive: per-feature percentile thresholds (CDF-uniform)
  • Gaussian: thresholds at quantiles of a fitted Normal(μ, σ) per feature
  • Exponential: log-spaced thresholds (good for long-tailed features)
  • Stochastic: coordinate-descent optimised thresholds per feature

Result: F4RM > Random across all 5 encoders.

3.3 — E8: Storage backend memory comparison¶

Two memory accountings for the same trained F4RM/Random WiSARD:

  • Dense hashmap — explicit (address → count) per RAM. Worst case 2^a × R bytes; in practice scales with the number of distinct training addresses observed.
  • Cuckoo filter (8-bit fingerprint, 0.95 load factor) — analytical storage proportional to the post-training distinct-address count.

This experiment quantifies the memory difference for matched accuracy.

3.4 — E9b: Heterogeneous-a F4RMS¶

Mixed-a F4RMS (10 members at each a in {4, 8, 16, 32, 64} for K=50 total) vs homogeneous F4RMS-50 at the principled-default a per dataset.

Caveat — small-feature datasets: For datasets where n_features × t < 64 (Iris, Seeds, Haberman, Ecoli, Balance Scale, Banknote), the heterogeneous list is per-dataset truncated to the a values that fit. The cell 53 patch in F4RM.ipynb implements this truncation; without it those datasets would silently produce empty results.

3.5 — E10: RAM selection¶

Two strategies for choosing which subset of RAMs to keep at inference time (after training a full ensemble):

  • Validation-driven: select RAMs whose individual validation accuracy exceeds a threshold.
  • Fisher score: rank RAMs by per-class Fisher discriminant score, keep top-K.

Both are evaluated against the trivial "keep all" baseline. The question: can we reduce inference cost without losing accuracy?

Summary¶

The robustness sweeps confirm:

  • The F4RM > Random win is stable across bleach (E6) and across five different thermometer encoders (E7).
  • The Cuckoo storage backend gives substantial memory savings vs dense hashmap at matched accuracy (E8).
  • F4RMS-K accuracy grows with K (E9a); heterogeneous-a F4RMS doesn't meaningfully beat homogeneous when a is well-chosen (E9b).
  • Validation-driven and Fisher-score RAM selection both reduce inference cost with minimal accuracy loss (E10).
  • Even with full per-dataset hyperparameter tuning (E11), F4RM beats the equivalently-tuned Random configuration on the majority of datasets.

Next: see F4RM_03_Comparisons_and_Pareto.ipynb for the Section 4 Pareto comparison vs tabular baselines and prior weightless systems.
